headline: Google freezes its bug bounty because of AI
dek: The program stopped after a flood of automated, invalid reports, according to TechCrunch and BleepingComputer.

s2.label: What happened
s2.title: New reports stopped coming in
body: Since October 1, Google no longer accepts new product vulnerability reports in OSS VRP, its reward program for open source software (TechCrunch, BleepingComputer).
The company cites “a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid.” The notice went out on X and on its Bug Hunters site (Help Net Security).

s3.label: How it works
s3.title: Every report needs a person
s3.body: Bounty programs pay people who find a security flaw before someone exploits it. But every submission has to be checked by hand.

points.t: Someone on the team or a project maintainer tries to repeat the issue described in the report.
If the flaw is not real, all the checking work is thrown away and the queue moves slower.
Engineers and maintainers were getting reports with details made up by AI (TechCrunch, citing Tom’s Hardware).

s4.label: Why it matters
s4.title: Sending got cheap, checking did not
body: OSS VRP has run since August 2022 and covers projects such as Go, Angular and Protocol Buffers (BleepingComputer).
The pause follows months of complaints about low-quality, AI-assisted reports hitting bounty programs and open source projects (Help Net Security). Google did not say how many it received.

items.t: Reports sent before the pause are still being processed (BleepingComputer, Help Net Security).
Cloud VRP and the Patch Rewards Program still accept reports (BleepingComputer, Infosecurity Magazine).
Google promises an update in the first quarter of 2027 and plans to restructure the program (Infosecurity Magazine).

caption.hook: Google froze OSS VRP, its bug bounty program for open source code, after a wave of AI-generated reports.
body: The program pays between $100 and $31,337 per flaw, depending on severity and how critical the project is, according to BleepingComputer and Infosecurity Magazine.

Supply chain reports, about how code is built and distributed, are not affected by the pause, according to BleepingComputer. Google is pointing researchers to its other programs while this one is on hold. Google has not said what filters the restructured program will use to keep automated reports out.
caption.cta: How should bug bounty programs separate real findings from automated reports?
